strengths: Conceptual Clarity and Novel Insight: The paper provides a fundamental and refreshing perspective on self-supervised novel view synthesis (NVS). By diagnosing that prior unposed methods (e.g., RayZer, RUST) often learn to interpolate context views rather than truly understand viewpoint transformation, the authors establish 'transferability' as the decisive criterion for genuine NVS.

Well-Motivated Technical Formulation: The proposed combination of a stereo-monocular setup (eliminating interpolation shortcuts) with pose-preserving augmentations (e.g., complementary masking across frame pairs) directly aligns the optimization objective with cross-scene transferability without relying on multi-view geometric priors or SE(3) parameterizations.

Thorough and Convincing Empirical Evaluation: The method is evaluated across four diverse real-world benchmarks (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2) against strong recent baselines. Under the newly introduced True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric, XFactor demonstrates dramatic improvements over RayZer and RUST.

Comprehensive Ablations: The ablation study cleanly demonstrates the necessity of each component, revealing counter-intuitive findings (e.g., that forcing explicit SE(3) parameterizations actually degrades transferability in unconstrained architectures, and that standard self-supervised objectives like SimCLR/VICReg fail to induce geometric awareness without rendering).

High Quality Presentation: The paper is exceptionally well-structured, clearly written, and provides thorough robustness analysis of the evaluation protocol (such as comparing VGGT and COLMAP oracles under corruptions).
weaknesses: Rendering Quality on Wide Baselines: As a deterministic feed-forward ViT renderer, XFactor produces noticeable blurring and warping artifacts under wide-baseline novel views or occluded regions, as acknowledged in the limitations.

Oracle Reliance for Evaluation: While the model itself is geometry-free and self-supervised, evaluating transferability via TPS relies on an external pretrained model (VGGT). Although the authors demonstrate VGGT's robustness over COLMAP, any systematic failure mode of the oracle could potentially influence the metric evaluation.
Minor Formatting and Placeholder Omissions: The abstract/introduction leaves 'Project Page:' blank, and Footnote 2 on page 16 has an empty URL placeholder.

strengths: Conceptual insight and framing: The paper provides a sharp, insightful conceptual distinction between frame interpolation and true novel view synthesis in the self-supervised regime, identifying cross-scene transferability of inferred camera poses as the key criterion.

Clever and elegant methodology: The proposed strategy—bootstrapping from a stereo-monocular formulation that forces extrapolation, paired with pose-preserving complementary masking augmentations to enforce the transferability objective—effectively resolves information leakage and pixel cheating without requiring complex geometric priors.

Intriguing 'geometry-free' finding: The paper demonstrates that unconstrained continuous latent vectors (256-D) can naturally learn transferable camera trajectories and align closely with SE(3) poses (as verified via linear probing), outperforming models forced into explicit SE(3) parameterizations and Plücker ray embeddings.

Thorough and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated across four diverse real-world datasets spanning both indoor scenes and objects (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2). The ablation study is comprehensive, testing encoder/decoder view counts, bottlenecking, temporal offsets, and alternative SSL losses (SimCLR, VICReg).
weaknesses: Reliance of TPS on an automated pose oracle: The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric depends on VGGT to extract camera trajectories from synthesized sequences. While VGGT is demonstrated to be more robust to corruptions than COLMAP (Table 8), deep-learning-based pose estimators might still exhibit inductive biases or drift on blurry/out-of-distribution neural renderings.

Rendering visual fidelity on wide baselines: Because XFactor is a deterministic feed-forward model trained with L1 + LPIPS, the rendered images often suffer from noticeable blurring and distortion artifacts when extrapolating to wider baselines or unobserved regions.

Pairwise pose estimation bottleneck: Restricting pose estimation to stereo pairs relative to a single chosen reference frame limits the system's ability to handle long-range or ultra-wide baseline camera motions where visual overlap with the reference frame is minimal.

strengths: Compelling conceptual framing: The paper clearly formalizes the limitation of prior self-supervised NVS methods (e.g., RayZer, RUST), showing that their latents primarily learn to interpolate context views rather than represent transferable camera trajectories, and identifies transferability as the defining criterion for true NVS.

Clever self-supervised formulation: The proposed training scheme combining a stereo-monocular design with pose-preserving complementary masking effectively circumvents information leakage and forces the network to learn relative camera pose representations without relying on explicit SE(3) parameterization or 3D inductive biases.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The method is validated across four diverse real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, and CO3Dv2) spanning both indoor/outdoor scenes and object-centric videos.

Rigorous ablations and diagnostic studies: The paper provides insightful analyses, including probing experiments mapping latent codes to SE(3) poses, comparisons with standard SSL objectives (SimCLR, VICReg), sensitivity to temporal shifts, and comparisons between VGGT and COLMAP for evaluation.
weaknesses: Augmentation gap during training: The pose-preserving augmentation relies on complementary masking and color jitter/blur of the same video pair. While this restricts pixel-level leakage across masks, the underlying underlying 3D geometry, global layout, and semantic content remain identical between Aug A and Aug B, meaning the network does not experience true cross-scene transfer during training.

Visual fidelity and reconstruction blurriness: Because the model is deterministic rather than generative, rendered views over wider baselines suffer from noticeable warping, blurriness, and loss of high-frequency details (as acknowledged in Section 5). While competitive in latent transferability metrics, perceptual rendering fidelity remains noticeably behind geometry-grounded or supervised methods.

Dependence on a deep learning oracle (VGGT) for evaluation: The TPS metric relies heavily on VGGT to extract camera trajectories from synthesized views. While VGGT is demonstrated to be more robust than COLMAP on distorted inputs, using a neural network oracle to benchmark another neural model could introduce systematic inductive biases or correlated failure modes.

Stereo bottleneck in multi-view reasoning: Multi-view extension still relies on a stereo pose encoder applied pairwise with respect to a heuristic reference frame ('middlest'), which limits the model's ability to reason about complex, multi-frame loop closures or ultra-wide baseline camera motions jointly.
Incomplete submission details: The manuscript contains missing links (e.g., empty 'Project Page:' on Page 1 and an empty Footnote 2 on Page 16).

strengths: Compelling conceptual framing: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes 'transferability' (re-rendering the same camera trajectory in an arbitrary novel scene) as the fundamental criterion for genuine novel view synthesis, exposing the context-interpolation failure mode prevalent in prior self-supervised NVS methods.

Clever and elegant methodology: Bootstrapping from a stereo-monocular setup (which strictly prevents interpolation) and enforcing a transferability objective using pose-preserving complementary/inverse masking is an insightful, geometry-free solution to prevent information leakage.

Strong and rigorous empirical evaluation: The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric provides a concrete way to measure trajectory transferability. Experiments across four diverse, large-scale benchmarks (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2) show substantial improvements over competitive baselines (RayZer and RUST).

Insightful ablations: The ablation study effectively supports the core hypotheses, demonstrating how end-to-end multi-view training degrades transferability and revealing the counter-intuitive result that explicit SE(3) parameterization harms performance compared to unconstrained latents trained under the transferability objective.
Probing experiments confirm that the unconstrained latent representation genuinely linearizes/captures SE(3) camera motion without hard-coded 3D inductive biases.
weaknesses: Re-implementation of baselines: Because neither RayZer nor RUST have publicly available official codebases, both were re-implemented by the authors. Although the authors verified their RayZer implementation with the original authors, slight architectural discrepancies remain (especially for RUST, as noted in Section 4).

Clarity on the multi-view fine-tuning stage: Section 3.5 briefly mentions multi-view fine-tuning, whereas Table 3 shows that adding views can sharply degrade transferability when trained end-to-end. A more detailed quantitative comparison between the pre-trained stereo-monocular model and the final fine-tuned multi-view model on the full benchmark would better clarify how much transferability is preserved during fine-tuning.

Artifacts under wide baselines: As acknowledged in the limitations, the model is a deterministic ViT-based regressor trained with L1 + LPIPS, which causes visible blurring and warping when extrapolating to wider baselines due to multi-modal uncertainty.

strengths: Compelling conceptual insight: The paper clearly articulates a fundamental flaw in existing self-supervised/pose-free NVS methods—namely, that multi-view autoencoding objectives encourage models to act as frame interpolators rather than learning controllable, transferable viewpoint representations.

Well-motivated formulation and metric: Formalizing novel view synthesis via transferability and introducing the True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric provides a standardized, principled way to evaluate whether pose-free representations actually capture camera geometry across scenes.

Elegant and effective method: The proposed XFactor approach—combining stereo-monocular bootstrapping with pose-preserving complementary mask augmentations—effectively bottlenecks information leakage without requiring explicit 3D inductive biases or handcrafted geometric priors.

Rigorous and comprehensive evaluation: The method is validated across four diverse real-world datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, and CO3Dv2). It dramatically outperforms prior self-supervised baselines (RayZer, RUST) on TPS and linear pose probing, while retaining competitive autoencoding fidelity.

Insightful ablations: The ablation study systematically dissects key design choices, demonstrating why multi-view end-to-end training collapses transferability and revealing the counter-intuitive observation that forcing an explicit SE(3) parameterization actually degrades latent transferability compared to the proposed objective.
weaknesses: Reliance on reimplemented baselines: Because neither RayZer nor RUST had released public code at submission time, comparisons rely on the authors' re-implementations. While the RayZer implementation was reportedly verified by its authors, the RUST variant incorporates architectural adjustments (e.g., absorbing the scene encoder into multi-view attention), which may introduce minor discrepancies from the original setting.

Evaluation dependence on external pose estimation: The proposed TPS metric depends on applying an external pose estimator (VGGT) to generated images. When rendered views exhibit noticeable blur or synthesis artifacts, the oracle pose estimator's predictions may degrade, potentially confounding pose error with perceptual fidelity.

Deterministic rendering limits on wide-baseline extrapolation: As acknowledged in the discussion, the deterministic ViT renderer can produce blurriness and warping artifacts when extrapolating across larger baselines, as it lacks a generative mechanism (e.g., diffusion/flow matching) to handle multi-modal perceptual uncertainty.

strengths: Compelling conceptual insight: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes a major failure mode in self-supervised NVS (the tendency of multi-view autoencoding models to interpolate context views rather than learning viewpoint-controllable rendering) and defines 'transferability' as the necessary criterion for true NVS.

Clever, geometry-free training strategy: The proposed solution—combining a stereo-monocular formulation (forcing extrapolation) with pose-preserving complementary masking augmentations to enable cross-pair transferability—is simple, elegant, and avoids hand-crafted 3D inductive biases.

Comprehensive evaluation across diverse benchmarks: The paper thoroughly tests on four major datasets (RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, CO3Dv2) spanning both object-centric and complex indoor/outdoor scenes, demonstrating drastic improvements over RayZer and RUST in transferability metrics.

Insightful probing and ablation studies: Probing experiments demonstrate that unconstrained latent poses naturally correlate strongly with ground-truth SE(3) camera poses. The ablations provide valuable, counter-intuitive findings (e.g., explicitly constraining the latent space to SE(3) and Plücker coordinates degrades transferability compared to unconstrained latents trained with the transferability objective).
weaknesses: Re-implementation nuances of prior work: Because source code for RayZer and RUST is not publicly available, both models were re-implemented. While the authors consulted the RayZer authors, the RUST baseline modifies key architectural elements (e.g., omitting the set-latent representation), which may introduce subtle confounders in baseline comparisons.

Dependence of the TPS metric on an external pose oracle: The proposed True Pose Similarity (TPS) metric relies on VGGT to extract camera trajectories from synthesized images. If novel views suffer from blurriness or artifacts under large extrapolations, the oracle's pose estimation accuracy could degrade and partially distort the TPS evaluation.

Deterministic rendering limits on wide baselines: As acknowledged in the limitations, the deterministic regression backbone struggles with large viewpoint changes and unobserved regions, leading to noticeable blurring and warping artifacts compared to modern generative 3D view synthesis models.
